name: Pipeline Orchestration
intent: Run a graph of data tasks in the right order, on a schedule, with retries, state tracking and safe re-runs.
scenario: A nightly pipeline for each date runs extract, clean, aggregate and publish. On March 3 the aggregate task dies halfway through writing its output, after 5 of 10 rows. Downstream tasks must not run on half a table, the failure must be visible, and re-running must not double-count.
problem: Data jobs depend on each other: clean needs extract, publish needs aggregate. A cron job per step has no idea whether its input exists, cannot retry only the part that broke, cannot backfill (re-process past dates) last month, and leaves no record of what ran. When one step fails silently, the next one runs on missing or partial data and the damage is found by a dashboard consumer days later.

howItWorks.title: Describe the pipeline as a DAG
howItWorks.text: A DAG (directed acyclic graph) is a set of tasks with one-way dependencies and no loops: tasks are nodes and dependencies are edges. The definition is code (Airflow, Dagster, Prefect, dbt's graph), so it is reviewed and versioned. The graph says what may run in parallel and what must wait, and nothing about when.

howItWorks.title: A scheduler creates runs per data interval
howItWorks.text: For a daily schedule the scheduler creates one run per logical date, with one task instance per task. The run for March 3 covers the data of March 3 and typically starts shortly after that day ends. The date is passed to the task, so the same code can be run for any day, which is what makes backfills possible.

howItWorks.title: Dispatch ready tasks to workers
howItWorks.text: A task is ready when all upstream instances succeeded. The scheduler places it on a queue limited by pools or slots (a typical Airflow default is 32 parallel tasks per installation), and a worker executes it. Every state change (queued, running, success, failed, upstream_failed) is written to a metadata database, which is the single source of truth.

howItWorks.title: Retry, then fail visibly
howItWorks.text: A failed attempt is retried after a delay, usually with exponential backoff (for example 2 minutes, then 4), up to a configured count, often 2 to 3. Retries absorb transient causes such as a throttled API or a lost connection. When retries are exhausted the instance is failed, its downstream instances are marked upstream_failed without running, and an alert fires.

howItWorks.title: Make tasks idempotent so re-runs are safe
howItWorks.text: Idempotent means running twice gives the same result as running once. A task that overwrites its own partition for its date (delete and insert in one transaction, or write a new file and swap it in) gives the same table after one run or five. An append-only task leaves the half-written rows of the dead attempt in place and adds a full set on top. Idempotence is what turns retry, clear-and-rerun and backfill into routine operations.

howItWorks.title: Recover and backfill by clearing state
howItWorks.text: The operator fixes the cause, then clears the failed task and its downstream instances, and the scheduler runs only those. A backfill creates runs for a past date range, bounded by a catchup or concurrency limit so that 90 old days do not swamp the cluster. Sensors (tasks that wait for data to arrive), SLAs (deadlines for finishing) and data-quality checks sit on top of the same graph.

pros: Dependencies are explicit, so a task never runs on input that does not exist yet
Failures are isolated and visible: a run page shows exactly which task and which date broke
Retries, timeouts, alerts and SLAs are configured once instead of in every script
Backfills and partial re-runs become a built-in operation instead of a weekend of manual work
The history of every run (duration, attempts, logs) is kept and queryable
cons: The scheduler and its metadata database become critical infrastructure that needs its own availability and upgrades
Scheduling is time-based and coarse: a daily DAG adds hours of latency compared with streaming
Correctness depends on every task being idempotent, which the orchestrator cannot check for you
Pipelines defined as code sprawl: hundreds of DAGs with implicit data dependencies across them are hard to reason about
Orchestrating is not processing: the heavy work still has to run in Spark, a warehouse or a container
whenToUse: Multi-step batch pipelines where later steps need the output of earlier ones
Jobs that need retries, alerting, run history and the ability to re-run a specific date
Work that spans systems (extract from an API, transform in a warehouse, publish to a BI tool) and needs one place to see it all
Regular backfills after bug fixes or late-arriving data
whenNotToUse: A single script that runs once a day and can simply be re-run: cron plus an alert is enough
Event-driven or low-latency flows, where a streaming job or a queue consumer is the right shape rather than a schedule
Per-record business workflows with long waits and compensations, which is the territory of sagas and workflow engines, not data orchestrators
Using the orchestrator to move data itself: tasks should trigger work in the right engine, not push gigabytes through the worker
pitfalls: Non-idempotent tasks: an append-only load plus a retry or backfill silently duplicates rows, and sums are inflated with no error
Using the wall clock instead of the logical date, so a re-run for March 3 processes today's data
Retrying a deterministic failure (bad schema, missing file) three times with backoff only delays the alert; retry transient errors and fail fast on the rest
Unbounded catchup or backfill that starts hundreds of runs at once and overwhelms the source database or the warehouse
Tasks that depend on data from another DAG without a sensor or dataset dependency, so they run before the upstream data lands
Passing large data through task-to-task messaging (XCom in Airflow) instead of storing it and passing a path
No timeout or SLA on a task: a hung task holds a slot forever and nothing alerts because nothing failed

roles.label: Scheduler
roles.description: Creates a run per data interval, decides which task instances are ready, and marks downstream tasks upstream_failed.

roles.label: Worker
roles.description: Executes one task attempt, typically by triggering work in an engine such as Spark or a warehouse.

roles.label: Metadata DB
roles.description: Stores the state of every run and task instance; the source of truth for the UI and the scheduler.

roles.label: Warehouse table
roles.description: The output the tasks write, partitioned by date.

roles.label: Operator
roles.description: The person who fixes the cause, clears failed tasks and starts backfills.

quiz.question: In a daily pipeline, the aggregate task for March 3 appends rows to a daily_totals table. It dies after writing 5 of its 10 rows, and the orchestrator retries it. The retry succeeds. How many rows for March 3 are in the table?
options: 10, because the orchestrator rolls back the failed attempt before retrying
10, because the retry only writes the 5 rows that are missing
5, because a retry that sees existing rows skips the write
15, because the 5 rows of the dead attempt stay and 10 more are added
quiz.explanation: An orchestrator reruns the task but does not undo its side effects. The orchestrator does not know which rows the dead attempt wrote, so it cannot write only the missing ones. Append-only tasks duplicate data on retry, so tasks should overwrite their own date partition, for example by delete and insert in one transaction.

quiz.question: A daily DAG task picks its data with WHERE day = date.today(). On March 10 an operator clears the failed March 3 run to re-run it. What data does the task process?
options: March 10 data, because it reads the wall clock instead of the logical date
March 3 data, because a cleared run remembers the date it was created for
No data, because the scheduler blocks re-runs of dates in the past
March 3 data, because the metadata database injects the run date into the SQL
quiz.explanation: Only a value passed in from the scheduler, the logical date, is tied to the run. Code that reads the clock behaves differently every time, which breaks re-runs and backfills.

quiz.question: A bug in the clean step is fixed, and the last 90 days of a daily DAG must be reprocessed. All tasks are idempotent. The source database handles about 4 concurrent extracts comfortably. What is the best way to do it?
options: Start all 90 runs at once and let the pool and worker slots queue them
Change the DAG to loop over 90 dates inside a single task
Run a backfill over the 90 dates, capped at about 4 concurrent runs
Run the script by hand in a shell loop, one date after another
quiz.explanation: A bounded backfill keeps per-date run history, retries and alerts, while the cap protects the source. Starting 90 runs at once can overwhelm it. A looped single task loses per-date visibility, and a manual loop loses retries and records altogether.
